easy.q: In Elder Renlund’s story, what was Mr. Martin upset about the day before he went home from the hospital?
options: His room was too noisy for sleeping
His breakfast was the wrong temperature
His family had come late to visit him
easy.why: After a miracle had saved his life, Mr. Martin said, “The oatmeal isn’t hot, and the milk isn’t cold!” He was looking only at his breakfast tray.

easy.q: In this talk, what does “cold oatmeal” stand for?
options: The everyday troubles in front of us that make us forget the bigger picture
The commandments that feel hard for us to keep when we are young
The blessings we were given but never remembered to share with others
easy.why: Elder Renlund said we can “focus on the here and now” and “lose sight of the bigger picture,” which includes where we have been and God’s promises to us.

easy.q: According to Elder Renlund, what did the children of Israel keep doing even though God’s miracles had saved them?
options: They tried to travel on without Moses
They stopped to build cities in the wilderness
They looked at their troubles and overlooked His blessings
easy.why: The Lord freed them, saved them at the Red Sea and fed them, “yet they repeatedly focused on cold oatmeal” and overlooked His blessings and promises.

easy.q: When Elder Renlund’s sister Linda read about promised blessings in the scriptures, what did she picture in her mind?
options: A big asterisk saying the blessings were for everyone except her
A long list of things she had to finish before any blessing came
A closed door that only the most faithful people could open
easy.why: Linda imagined a big asterisk that left her out. Elder Renlund taught that “there is no asterisk excluding you from God’s richest blessings.”

easy.q: What did Elder Renlund ask us to strive to remember, especially when we face “cold oatmeal”?
options: The times we solved hard problems on our own
The times the Lord has listened to us
The times other people had bigger troubles
easy.why: He said to remember “all the times He has inclined His ear to you.” Remembering how the Lord has heard us helps us trust His promises.

medium.q: Why did Elder Renlund tell the story of Mr. Martin and his breakfast?
options: To show that complaining keeps promised blessings from coming to us
To show that miracles usually come only after a very long wait
To show how daily challenges can make us lose sight of the bigger picture
To show that those who serve the sick need patience with them
medium.why: Elder Renlund said we “can easily fall into the same trap,” focusing on the here and now and forgetting where we have been and God’s promises to us.

medium.q: The Lord asked Moses, “how long will it be ere they believe me?” According to Elder Renlund, what was the Lord asking?
options: Why His people would not trust Him despite all He had done
How long His people must wander before they would obey
When His people would stop asking Him for more signs
Whether His people would ever thank Moses for leading them
medium.why: Elder Renlund put the Lord’s question in other words: “Despite all I have done, why won’t they believe me?” It is a question about trust.

medium.q: The Savior said, “I have overcome the world.” What did Elder Renlund say this means for us?
options: The faithful will be spared tribulation in this life
We must overcome the world in the same way He did
The troubles of the world will soon come to an end
We do not have to overcome the world ourselves
medium.why: Elder Renlund taught, “Jesus overcame the world; we do not have to do so ourselves.” Tribulation still comes, but He promises spiritual peace.

medium.q: Elder Renlund quoted Lehi telling his son Jacob that he was redeemed. What did Elder Renlund use this to show?
options: Faithful parents can be certain their children will be redeemed
Redemption comes through the Redeemer’s righteousness, not our own
Jacob had earned his redemption by being good and faithful
Redemption is promised to those who suffer much while young
medium.why: Jacob was good and faithful, yet Lehi said he was redeemed “because of the righteousness of thy Redeemer.” Elder Renlund said the same is true for each of us.

medium.q: According to Elder Renlund, what happens as we reflect on the great things the Lord has already done?
options: We earn greater blessings than we had before
Our day-to-day challenges begin to go away
We are better able to rely on His promises
We no longer need to ask Him for help
medium.why: Remembering His goodness and mercy leaves us “better positioned to grasp the bigger picture and to rely on His promises to us.”

hard.q: Elder Renlund said the “bigger picture” Mr. Martin lost sight of that morning had two parts. What were they?
options: His wife’s sacrifice and the skill of his doctors
Where he had been and the promise his future held
The donor’s gift and the cost of his long care
His past mistakes and the blessings he now enjoyed
hard.why: Mr. Martin forgot “both where he had been and the promise the future now held.” Elder Renlund then applied the same two parts to us: where we have been and God’s promises.

hard.q: At the edge of the promised land, Israel wished they had died in Egypt. Which thought today is most like what Elder Renlund said lay behind their words?
options: God has helped me before, so I need not do anything myself
This trial must be a punishment for something I have done
Others are promised blessings that were never meant for me
Life was easier before, and this problem is beyond even God
hard.why: Elder Renlund explained that “they thought that they had it better before” and that the challenge ahead was surely too much, even for the Lord.

hard.q: Linda said, “I am not extraordinary enough to warrant an exception.” Which statement best explains her reasoning?
options: Being left out would take being a special case, and she is not one
Being blessed takes extraordinary faith, which she had now gained
Being ordinary means receiving smaller blessings than others do
Being patient for many years had finally earned her a place
hard.why: Her point was that the promises have no exceptions: “The blessings are promised to me too.” Elder Renlund added that Linda is extraordinary “but still no exception.”

hard.q: Which belief does Elder Renlund’s explanation of “ample provision” most directly correct?
options: My blessings would come sooner if I were more diligent
My trials are heavier than those of the people around me
What I lack is more than the Savior’s power can make up
My daily troubles keep me from seeing past blessings
hard.why: “Ample provision” means “all human circumstances are within the Savior’s redemptive reach.” His power is “more than enough to cover any breach, need, or deficit.”

hard.q: Which person best fits what Elder Renlund taught about peace and joy in our “here and now”?
options: Someone who finally feels peace once a long trial has ended
Someone who finds joy by choosing to ignore present troubles
Someone who feels better after noticing that others have it worse
Someone still in a hard trial who has peace through faith in Christ
hard.why: When our faith is centered on Jesus Christ, “He promises spiritual peace no matter our circumstances.” The peace comes because of Him, while the trial may remain.
